source.title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
source.summary: Modern LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenHands share a common inefficiency: they spend much of their token budget finding the file to patch, rather than patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, with many calls spent on grep, glob, and view_file during repository exploration. We introduce CodeGrep, a 14B retrieval agent trained end-to-end with GRPO to issue multi-turn parallel grep, glob, and read tool calls and return candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent. On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep preserves resolve rate while substantially improving efficiency: 27.0% versus 25.8% for the no-retrieval baseline, with 15% fewer rounds and 19% fewer tokens on resolved instances. Across retrievers, downstream utility follows a precision threshold: BM25 with precision 0.375 degrades the agent, Jina with precision 0.445 is neutral, and CodeGrep with precision 0.677 crosses the threshold at which retrieval begins to reduce rollout cost. To enable this study, we mine supervision from 67K open-source agent trajectories using CATM and build a Git-worktree environment for multi-turn agent RL. In our setting, applying the efficiency signal at the advantage layer rather than the reward layer reduces KL drift and translates cleanly into downstream efficiency. We will release the model, training pipeline, RL environment, and evaluation harnesses.

previous_facts.title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
previous_facts.event_hint: CodeGrep: a 14B agent-style code retriever trained end-to-end with GRPO and injected into a frozen OpenHands agent on SWE-Bench Verified to cut exploration rounds and tokens.
previous_facts.problem: Modern LLM coding agents (Claude Code, OpenHands) spend most of their token budget finding the file to patch rather than writing the patch. A 30B OpenHands agent on SWE-Bench Verified averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, dominated by grep, glob and view_file calls in ambiguous exploration loops, often 20+ rounds in a wrong direction before giving up. Whether a specialized retrieval submodule can shorten this exploration phase (H2: same issues resolved with shorter rollout) without hurting resolve (H1: better retrieval raises resolve) had not been jointly tested in the open.
previous_facts.mechanism: CodeGrep is a 14B retriever built on Qwen3-14B-Instruct, trained end-to-end with GRPO (on ms-swift, LoRA + optimizer offload + vLLM-colocated rollout on a single 8xB200 node, ~27h wall-clock, early-stopped at step 897 of 2000). It exposes three read-only primitives (grep regex search, glob path matching, read file contents) and emits up to 8 parallel tool calls per turn executed concurrently inside a Git-worktree RL environment, capped at 4 turns (3 exploration + 1 answer), max 32 tool execs per rollout. Supervision is mined from 67K open-source OpenHands trajectories via CATM (one-to-many attribution), giving 31,977 effective training samples (47.7% retention) judged by GLM-5.1-FP8 (16-way parallel, ~5h). At inference, CodeGrep takes the issue description, emits a candidate-file list injected into the prompt of a frozen downstream OpenHands agent (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507) — only the retriever is trained, so downstream effects attribute cleanly. Reward-design study v1->v2->v3 shows moving the efficiency signal from the reward layer to the advantage layer holds KL drift to ~0.09-0.15 vs v1's ~0.31, and v3 drops an auxiliary line-range term absent from the downstream editor.

evidence.claim: Injected into a frozen OpenHands agent on all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep v3 lifts resolve rate by +1.2pp (25.8% -> 27.0%) while cutting resolved rounds 23.0 -> 19.6 (-15%) and resolved tokens 631K -> 514K (-19%).
evidence.baseline: no-retrieval baseline (OpenHands Qwen3-30B-A3B, 25.8% resolve at 23.0 rounds / 631K tokens per resolved issue)
evidence.condition: SWE-Bench Verified, 500 instances, frozen OpenHands + Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 at temp 0, 100-round max

evidence.claim: Across three retrievers, downstream utility follows a precision threshold with three regimes: BM25 at file-precision 0.375 degrades the agent (resolve -0.6pp, resolved tokens +21% to 763K); Jina-1.5B at precision 0.445 is neutral (resolve 25.8%, tokens -7% to 587K); CodeGrep at precision 0.677 crosses the threshold at which retrieval begins to buy efficiency.
evidence.value: BM25 0.375 hurts; Jina 0.445 neutral; CodeGrep 0.677 buys efficiency
evidence.condition: SWE-Bench Verified, frozen OpenHands agent; file-precision on internal eval set (Table 2)
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 6 (Section 4.3 + Section 5.1 precision threshold); PDF Page 6 Table 2

evidence.claim: BM25 injection restricted to the 94 instances both configs resolve spends 6.6% more rounds and 38.6% more tokens than baseline, confirming below-threshold retrieval actively harms efficiency.
evidence.condition: 94 instances resolved by both BM25-injected and baseline configs

evidence.claim: Reward-design study: applying the tool-call efficiency signal at the advantage layer (v2/v3) instead of multiplicative reward-layer scaling (v1) reduces KL-to-reference drift from ~0.31 to 0.09/0.15; v3 also stabilizes average tool-use turns at ~2.1 vs v1/v2 rebounding to ~2.6 after step 500.
evidence.value: KL 0.31 -> 0.09/0.15; tool turns stabilize ~2.1 vs rebound ~2.6
evidence.condition: GRPO training of CodeGrep, ~900-step run, Fig. 2
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 5 (Section 3.6 Training dynamics); PDF Page 6 Fig. 2

evidence.claim: CodeGrep v3 retrieval quality on internal eval: F-beta mean 0.576, F-beta median 0.714, precision 0.677, recall 0.435, 43.0% of cases with F-beta >= 0.8, in 2.3 turns; vs BM25 precision 0.375 and Jina-1.5B precision 0.445.
evidence.value: v3 F-beta 0.576 mean / 0.714 median; precision 0.677; recall 0.435; 43.0% F-beta>=0.8; 2.3 turns
evidence.condition: internal retrieval-quality evaluation set, agentic retriever turns column (Table 2)
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 6 (Table 2: Retrieval quality on the internal evaluation set)

previous_facts.evaluation_context: Benchmark: SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances). Downstream agent: OpenHands with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 at temperature 0, 100-round max, frozen. Baseline reproduces public reference: 25.8% resolve at 23.0 rounds / 631K tokens per resolved issue (within 1 SD of publicly reported 25.2 +/- 0.7%). Six configs compared: baseline, BM25, Jina-1.5B, CodeGrep v1/v2/v3. Training: GRPO on ms-swift, LoRA + optimizer offload + vLLM-colocated rollout, single 8xB200 node, ~27h wall-clock, early-stop step 897 of planned 2000. RL environment: thousands of unique (repo,commit) pairs after dedup, bare repo + worktree per rollout, tool concurrency cap 64 (asyncio), max 8 parallel tools per turn, max 32 tool execs per rollout (4 turns x 8). Data: 67,074 raw trajectories -> 31,977 effective training samples (47.7% retention) judged by GLM-5.1-FP8 (16-way parallel, ~5h stage runtime).
previous_facts.limitations: Resolve-rate lift is small (+1.2pp, 25.8%->27.0%) and CodeGrep v1 reaches the same 27.0% resolve without the efficiency gain, so the resolve contribution is not clearly attributable to v3 specifically. Efficiency is reported only on resolved instances (rounds/tokens per resolved issue) and the paper flags a methodological caveat on efficiency accounting in section 5.3 (not fully visible). Training is single-node, early-stopped at step 897 of a 2000-step budget, so full-budget behavior is unknown. Downstream utility is characterized only for OpenHands + Qwen3-30B-A3B; the authors conjecture (Appendix B) that agents whose editor consumes line ranges (e.g. Windsurf Cascade) may benefit from the line-range term that v3 drops, while file-level editors (OpenHands, Cursor) do not — but this is a conjecture, not measured. Closed commercial comparator Cognition SWE-grep has an undisclosed reward formulation, so component-level comparison is partial. Model release is promised ('we will release') but not yet public at paper time.
previous_facts.project_relevance: Directly on-topic for the agent-acceleration card's central question of reducing repeated Read/Grep/Glob and shortening the exploration phase: CodeGrep is a concrete, open, RL-trained retrieval submodule that delivers a measured -15% rounds / -19% tokens efficiency dividend on a real SWE-Bench Verified workload while preserving resolve, with the downstream agent frozen so the gain attributes to the retriever. The precision-threshold characterization (BM25 0.375 hurts, Jina 0.445 neutral, CodeGrep 0.677 buys efficiency) is project-actionable: it gives a concrete precision bar (~0.677) that a code retriever must clear before it reduces rollout cost, and it warns that naive lexical retrieval actively harms efficiency. The advantage-layer vs reward-layer RL finding is a reusable design rule for training future tool-using retrieval agents.

evidence_gaps.question: What does Section 5.3's methodological caveat on efficiency accounting say (efficiency is reported only on resolved instances — is there an unresolved-instance or aggregate accounting that changes the magnitude)?
